title: Why Memory Comes in Layers
objective: After this level you can explain why a computer keeps data in layers, from tiny fast cache to roomy RAM to big slow storage.
summary: Main memory is far slower than the processor, so memory comes in layers: registers and SRAM cache on the chip, denser DRAM main memory, then cheap storage.

cards.headline: Your processor is faster than its own memory.
cards.body: A processor can do a sum in a nanosecond or less. Fetching a number from main memory typically takes 20 to 80 nanoseconds. Level 8's loop fetches all the time, so without a plan the fastest part of the computer would spend most of its time waiting.

cards.headline: Three layers, from quick to roomy

items.label: On the processor chip
points: Registers: a small number, very fast
Cache: fast SRAM, up to several megabytes
Holds what is being used right now

items.label: Main memory (RAM)
points: DRAM: slower, but several times denser
Loses everything when the power goes off

items.label: Storage
points: Keeps your files with the power off

cards.headline: Why not make it all fast?
cards.body: Because fast memory costs space and money. Cache is made of SRAM, which is quick but physically large: a chip the same size holds several times as much of the slower DRAM used for main memory. So memory comes as a hierarchy, from fast, expensive registers inside the processor down to slower, cheaper storage. Think of a desk, a bookshelf and a warehouse.

cards.headline: Why a small cache is enough
cards.body: Programs are creatures of habit. They repeat the same instructions in loops and work on related data, a pattern called locality of reference. So once values are copied from main memory into the cache, many later requests find them already there. A cache of up to several megabytes near the processor takes a lot of the waiting out of the loop.

mascot.line: This connects to Level 8: every fetch asks memory for something. Cache keeps many of those trips short.

cards.headline: Memory: layered
learned: Main memory is far slower than the processor
Registers and SRAM cache sit on the chip; DRAM is denser but slower
Storage is slowest and cheapest, and keeps data with the power off
Programs reuse data, so a small cache helps a lot

options.label: On the processor chip, as fast SRAM
On the hard drive, as spare space
options.rationale: Storage is the slowest layer, far from the processor.

options.label: In the internet's routers
options.rationale: Cache here means memory inside your own computer.

options.label: In the screen, beside the pixels
options.rationale: The screen displays; it is not the processor's memory.

questions.explanation: Cache is fast SRAM on the processor chip, up to several megabytes.

questions.prompt: Why can a cache of just a few megabytes speed up a much bigger program?

options.label: It compresses the whole program to fit
options.rationale: Cache keeps copies of values; it does not compress programs.

options.label: It stores the program permanently with the power off
It makes main memory itself run faster
options.rationale: Main memory stays just as slow.

options.label: Programs keep reusing the same instructions and related data

questions.explanation: Locality of reference: loops repeat instructions and use related data, so copies in cache get reused.

questions.prompt: Level 8's processor fetches from memory on every cycle. Why does a 20 to 80 nanosecond memory delay matter?

options.label: Memory access resets the program counter
options.rationale: Access time does not change the counter.

options.label: The processor can finish an operation in a nanosecond or less, so it would wait
The clock stops completely during every fetch
options.rationale: The clock keeps ticking at a fixed rate.

options.label: Slow memory changes the values it stores
options.rationale: Slow memory is late, not wrong.

questions.explanation: Main memory is many times slower than the processor, which is why caches exist.
